questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: separate a question about generalising from a question about the comparison
questions.stem: A trial finds a new writing programme raises essay scores in the eight classes that took it. Which question does this design leave open?

options.text: Whether those eight classes can stand in for all learners
Whether the classes already differed before the programme began
options.misconception: calls a question about generalising a question about the comparison inside the study

options.text: Whether the score gain is larger than the random scatter around it
options.misconception: turns a generalising problem into a problem of sampling scatter

options.text: Whether the essay score measured quality as the study defined it
options.misconception: treats a question about who the results cover as a question about the measure

questions.explanation: External validity asks whether a result travels beyond the people and settings that produced it, and eight volunteer classes in one school may be unlike most classrooms in age, ability, and staffing. Whether those classes began alike is an internal validity question, whether the gain exceeds random scatter is a conclusion validity question, and whether the score captured the intended quality is a measurement question, none of which is the open issue here.
questions.hint: Ask what the study has not yet established about people it never studied.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the multiple-comparisons problem among the usual four
questions.stem: Four separate problems weaken the step from data to conclusion. Which one describes the multiple-comparisons problem?

options.text: Testing many outcomes, so some look significant purely by chance
Group sizes that differ, leaving the comparison unbalanced overall
options.misconception: describes unequal group sizes rather than repeated testing

options.text: An instrument that folds two constructs into a single score
options.misconception: names a measurement fault as though it were a testing fault

options.text: A comparison group picked because it was the nearest one available
options.misconception: names a selection problem as though it were a testing problem

questions.explanation: The multiple-comparisons problem is arithmetic on a family of tests: if thirty outcomes are each tested at a 5 percent level, a handful will look significant even when nothing is happening, and reporting only those hands the reader a family-wise error rate of about 0.79. Unequal group sizes are a precision problem, an instrument covering two constructs is a measurement problem, and grabbing the nearest available comparison group is a selection problem.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four has nothing to do with the sample and everything to do with how many tests were run.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state what differential loss to follow-up does to a longitudinal result
questions.stem: A year-long study finds that the participants who drop out are less satisfied than those who stay to the end. What has happened to the result?

options.text: Attrition bias, since who remained no longer resembles who began
Nothing, since losses and new recruits are expected to cancel
options.misconception: assumes people leaving and people joining balance one another out

options.text: Precision alone, since the group that stayed is smaller than planned
options.misconception: confuses a changed sample with a wider margin of error

options.text: Maturation, since a year of change has altered everyone's scores
options.misconception: relabels a selection effect as a change every participant underwent

questions.explanation: Attrition matters when leaving is related to the measured variable, and here the leavers are systematically less satisfied, so the final analysis describes a happier subgroup than the one that started, which is a selection effect created by who remained. A smaller sample widens the interval but says nothing about composition, and a year of change would have shifted everyone's scores rather than thinning the sample in a biased direction.
questions.hint: Ask what the leavers have in common, not how many of them there are.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise a group difference that exists before treatment begins
questions.stem: Two groups are compared on the outcome measure before any treatment is applied and they already differ by 8 points. What is this?

options.text: A selection effect, since the groups were not equivalent at the start
A history effect, since something outside the study shifted the scores
options.misconception: labels a difference present at the start as an event during the study

options.text: A testing effect, since the first measuring pass moved the scores already
options.misconception: blames the pre-test for a gap that existed before it was given

options.text: A maturation effect, since time passing altered the two groups differently
options.misconception: relabels a starting difference as a change the groups underwent

questions.explanation: A selection effect is a difference between groups that is already there when the study begins, so any later gap has to be read on top of 8 points that had nothing to do with the treatment. A history event would be something that happened during the study, being measured for the first time cannot create a gap that preceded the measurement, and maturation describes change the participants undergo over time rather than a difference they brought with them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the gap was present before anything was done to either group.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise an outside event that could move the outcome by itself
questions.stem: A study runs for six weeks and a heat wave passes through, affecting every participant the same way. What threatens the result?

options.text: A history event, since an outside change could move the scores alone
Maturation, since everyone improves steadily over a six-week interval
options.misconception: calls an outside event a change every participant undergoes

options.text: A testing effect, since the first measuring pass made the scores unusual
options.misconception: blames the pre-test for a change the weather produced

options.text: A selection effect, since the heat drove some participants out of the study
options.misconception: invents participants leaving where the scenario reports none leaving

questions.explanation: A history effect is anything outside the study that happens to both groups during it, and a heat wave can depress attention and scores on its own, so any change over the six weeks is no longer attributable to the intervention. Maturation would be development the participants undergo by themselves, being measured once cannot manufacture a weather effect, and the scenario reports everyone staying, so nobody has been selected out.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the participants that the researchers did not arrange.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise ordinary development as an explanation for a rise over time
questions.stem: Children's puzzle scores are recorded twice six months apart with no programme introduced, and both times the scores are higher. What accounts for the rise?

options.text: Maturation, since the children develop across the interval anyway
Testing, since solving the puzzles once made the second sitting easier
options.misconception: credits ordinary development to having been measured once

options.text: History, since the school changed its timetable over the interval
options.misconception: invents a timetable change the scenario does not report

options.text: Regression, since the first high scores must pull the second set down
options.misconception: predicts a fall where the reported scores rose

questions.explanation: Children genuinely get better at puzzles simply by getting older, so scores rising with no programme present is maturation and would happen in any group left alone, which is why such a design needs a comparison group measured on the same schedule. Practising the puzzles once makes the second sitting easier, but nothing here indicates a timetable change, and regression pulls extreme high scores down, while these scores rose.
questions.hint: Ask whether the children would have improved even if nobody had measured them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: recognise the gain produced by having been measured once already
questions.stem: Students solve a short puzzle, then six weeks later solve what they are told is a different but equally hard one, and they do better. Why?

options.text: The testing effect, since solving once made the second task familiar
Maturation, since half a year of practice improves puzzle solving
options.misconception: credits ordinary development instead of the earlier practice

options.text: A placebo effect, since the students expect to have improved by now
options.misconception: treats improvement between sittings as an expectation effect

options.text: Regression, since a high first score must be followed by a lower one
options.misconception: expects a fall in the second score rather than the reported rise

questions.explanation: Practising a task makes the second attempt easier for reasons that have nothing to do with any programme, so the testing effect means the pre-test itself supplies some of the gain and a design must separate that from the treatment. Half a year does make children better at puzzles, but the effect named here is the practice carried over from the first sitting, and nothing about expectation produces a real gain on a new puzzle.
questions.hint: Ask what the students got out of the first sitting that carries into the second.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a second extreme reading is usually milder
questions.stem: Patients are enrolled because a first blood-pressure reading came out unusually high, and at the next visit most read lower. Why?

options.text: Regression to the mean, since an extreme tends to be followed by milder
The treatment working, since the second reading is below the first
options.misconception: credits the treatment for a drop that selection alone predicts

options.text: Maturation, since patients relax as the study carries on
options.misconception: explains a statistical artefact as gradual personal change

options.text: A placebo effect, since taking part in the study reassures them
options.misconception: attributes an artefact of selection to reassurance from participating

questions.explanation: Selecting on an extreme reading guarantees a group whose readings include real error as well as real hypertension, and on a second occasion that error does not repeat, so the average falls without anything having been treated, which is regression to the mean. It makes an untreated comparison group look better and a treated group look better for the same reason, and no amount of relaxation or reassurance enters the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the random error that helped pick these patients in the first place.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish being watched from believing a remedy works
questions.stem: How does behaving differently because one is being observed at work differ from behaving differently because one believes a remedy works?

options.text: The observer changes behaviour, while the remedy changes it through belief
Both are expectation effects, since being watched is itself a belief
options.misconception: collapses the observer and the believed remedy into one cause

options.text: One is a physical influence, while the other is only a belief
options.misconception: treats the two as different in kind rather than in cause

options.text: Neither runs through expectation, since both follow simply from study
options.misconception: denies that either effect depends on what participants expect

questions.explanation: The observer effect is triggered by the presence of an evaluator, so the worker changes pace or effort because of who is watching, and it would occur with no treatment in the picture at all. A placebo effect runs through the participant's belief that something active has been given, so it needs a treatment to believe in, and keeping the two apart matters because an observer effect inflates every condition in a study while a placebo effect inflates only the arm that received an inert version.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two can happen with no treatment involved anywhere.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why many tests at one level inflate false positives
questions.stem: A team tests 30 outcome measures, each at the conventional 5 percent level, and reports only the 3 that came out significant. What is wrong?

options.text: A family of tests that size produces false positives by chance alone
Thirty tests is a small number, so three hits is an expected count
options.misconception: judges a family of tests by what a single test would produce

options.text: Only the significant results are real, so the other 27 were mistakes
options.misconception: keeps whichever results cleared the bar and discards the rest as error

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since 5 percent applies to each test taken alone
options.misconception: applies the per-test threshold while ignoring the family it belongs to

questions.explanation: Run thirty times at a 5 percent level with nothing real going on, the chance of at least one hit is one minus 0.95 to the thirtieth, which is about 0.79, so roughly six of those thirty would have looked significant by luck and reporting the lucky ones is indistinguishable from cherry-picking. The per-test threshold is a property of a single test, and once tests are run as a family the budget has to cover the family or be corrected.
questions.hint: Ask what the chance is of at least one hit when nothing at all is happening.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the chance of at least one false positive in a family of tests
questions.stem: A report runs 20 independent significance tests, each at a 5 percent level, and nothing real is going on. What is the approximate chance that at least one of them comes out significant purely by chance? Report the proportion only.
questions.explanation: The chance that every one of the 20 tests misses is 0.95 raised to the 20th, which is 0.3585, so the chance that at least one hits by luck alone is 1 minus that, or 0.6415. Adding the 20 per-test rates would give more than 1 and answer nothing, and treating each test as a separate 5 percent event is exactly the error that lets two thirds of such families produce a headline.
questions.hint: Find the chance that none of them hits, then take the complement.

provenance.author: bank-team-resmeth

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the per-test threshold that holds a family at one level
questions.stem: A family of 20 tests must be held to an overall 5 percent level using a Bonferroni adjustment. What per-test threshold does that require? Report the proportion only.
questions.explanation: The Bonferroni rule spends the family budget evenly, so 0.05 divided across 20 tests leaves 0.0025 for each one, which is what keeps the chance of at least one false positive across the family at 0.05. Leaving each test at 0.05 would let that chance climb to 0.6415, and the price of the correction is honest: each test becomes harder to declare significant, so real effects can be missed.
questions.hint: Divide the overall level by the number of tests in the family.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute a standardised mean difference from two group means
questions.stem: A trial reports a treatment group mean of 78.4 and a comparison group mean of 71.2 on a measure whose pooled standard deviation is 12. What is the standardised mean difference?
questions.explanation: The standardised mean difference divides the gap between the means by the pooled standard deviation, and 78.4 minus 71.2 is 7.2 raw points, so 7.2 over 12 is 0.60, which says the gap is six tenths of one pooled deviation. Leaving 7.2 as the answer ties the effect to the units of the instrument, and dividing by the sample size instead of the standard deviation produces a number that means nothing at all.
questions.hint: Subtract the two means, then divide by the pooled standard deviation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the shared share of variation from a correlation
questions.stem: Two measures are reported with a correlation of 0.62. What share of the variation in one of them is shared with the other, expressed as a proportion?
questions.explanation: The shared share is the correlation squared, so 0.62 times 0.62 is 0.3844, which puts the shared variation at a little under 38 percent. Using 0.62 directly would claim 62 percent is shared, which overstates the overlap because the relationship is not a straight line through the origin, and the remaining variation belongs to other influences this pair of measures does not capture.
questions.hint: Square the correlation to get the shared share of variation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the width of a reported confidence interval
questions.stem: A difference in mean scores is reported with a 95 percent interval running from 4.2 to 9.8 points. How wide is that interval? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The width runs from one end of the interval to the other, so 9.8 minus 4.2 is 5.6 points, and the midpoint of 7.0 is the estimate that width is measured around. Measuring from the estimate out to one end would give 2.8, which is the margin of error rather than the width, and a wide interval means the true difference is pinned down less tightly than a narrow one would leave it.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower end of the interval from the upper end.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute a correlation from a small set of pairs
questions.stem: Five pairs of values are recorded: the first variable takes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and the second takes 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. What is their correlation? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The two means are 3 and 4, the products of the deviations sum to 6, and the squared deviations sum to 10 for the first variable and 6 for the second, so the correlation is 6 over the square root of 60, which is 0.7746. A perfect 1.0 would need the second value to climb with the first at every step, and here 4 appears at two different first-variable values, which is what holds the figure below 1.
questions.hint: Take the means, then divide the summed products of deviations by the root of the two squared-deviation sums.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute an absolute difference between two event rates
questions.stem: In a trial the recorded event occurs in 68 percent of the treated group and 52 percent of the comparison group. What is the absolute difference between these two rates?
questions.explanation: An absolute difference subtracts the two rates directly, and 0.68 minus 0.52 is 0.16, which is 16 percentage points of events attached to the treatment in this sample. Reading the two rates as a ratio would answer a different question about relative change, and 0.16 by itself says nothing about how many people a 16 point shift matters to without knowing how common the event is to begin with.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller rate from the larger one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the degrees of freedom for a within-person comparison
questions.stem: The same 42 participants are measured on an outcome before and after a programme, and the analysis compares each person's two readings with each other. How many degrees of freedom does that paired comparison have?
questions.explanation: A paired comparison works on the difference within each person, and 42 people supply 42 such differences, so one goes to estimating the overall average difference and 41 remain to vary, which is the count of degrees of freedom. Reporting 42 would count people instead of independent pieces of information, and 83 would be the figure for two unrelated groups of 42, which is a different comparison and a different assumption.
questions.hint: Count the paired differences, then subtract one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of a study sample retained to the end
questions.stem: A study enrolls 480 participants and 372 are still measured at the final appointment. What percentage of those enrolled were retained through to the end?
questions.explanation: Retention divides the people measured at the end by the people who started, and 372 over 480 is 0.775, which is 77.5 percent, with the 108 who left making up the 22.5 percent difference. Taking the 372 as a share of a completed group instead would leave nobody in the denominator, and a retention figure on its own says nothing about whether the leavers differed from those who stayed.
questions.hint: Divide the number measured at the end by the number who were enrolled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.learningObjective: recover a standardised difference from a test statistic and group sizes
questions.stem: A test comparing two equal groups of 50 participants returns a test statistic of 2.20, and the two group means differ by 4.4 points. What is the standardised mean difference?
questions.explanation: With 50 people in each group the two reciprocal sample sizes sum to 0.04, whose square root is 0.2, so the standardised difference is 2.20 times 0.2, which is 0.44, and the raw gap of 4.4 points over a pooled deviation of 10 gives the same figure. Reading 2.20 as the effect size would be reporting a statistic that grows with the sample size rather than a measure of how big the gap is.
questions.hint: Use the square root of the sum of the reciprocals of the two group sizes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state what a p-value does and does not describe
questions.stem: A test returns a value of 0.03. Which statement reads that number correctly?

options.text: With nothing going on, results this extreme arise about 3 times in 100
There is a 3 percent chance this particular result was a fluke
options.misconception: reads the value as the chance that this result itself was a fluke

options.text: There is a 97 percent chance that the conclusion is correct
options.misconception: turns the value into a confidence level for the conclusion

options.text: The finding will replicate in about 97 studies out of 100
options.misconception: treats the value as a forecast of how often a study repeats

questions.explanation: A p-value describes how often results this extreme would appear if the tested claim were true, so 0.03 means such results would turn up in about 3 of every 100 repetitions under that assumption. It is not the chance that this particular result was luck, and it is not a 97 percent probability that the conclusion is right, because the probability attaches to the data-generating assumption rather than to the conclusion or to whether the study repeats.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen if the claim being tested were true and nothing else was.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the two quantities that set a confidence interval's width
questions.stem: Two studies estimate the same difference, and the one with five times the participants reports a far narrower interval. What sets the width?

options.text: The spread of the measure and the size of the sample
The spread of the measure alone, which the larger study also had
options.misconception: ignores the sample size that also drives the width

options.text: The size of the effect, so a bigger study must have found more
options.misconception: reads the width as a report of how large the effect is

options.text: The convention chosen, so authors report whichever suits them
options.misconception: treats a computed interval as a free choice for the author

questions.explanation: The width follows from the spread of the measure and the sample size together, because the standard error divides the spread by the root of the sample size, so five times the participants cuts the width by about the root of five. The width says how tightly this sample pins the estimate and nothing about how big the effect is, and no author chooses it after the fact, since it is computed from the data and the method.
questions.hint: Ask which two quantities appear in the standard error.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: separate the question a test answers from the question a size answers
questions.stem: Why does a report give an effect size alongside its significance test rather than the test alone?

options.text: The test asks whether noise could explain it, the size says how much
The size replaces the test, since a large effect is always detected
options.misconception: treats a large effect as automatically detectable at any sample size

options.text: The size settles whether the design was valid, which the test cannot
options.misconception: assigns the validity question to the effect size alone

options.text: The size is needed first, since the test statistic is computed from it
options.misconception: reverses the dependency between the test and the effect size

questions.explanation: A significance test answers whether a gap is large enough to stand out from random scatter at this sample size, and that verdict moves with n, so a very large study can detect a difference too small to act on. The effect size stays put as the sample grows and reports the gap itself, and neither of them says anything about whether the design could support a causal claim, which is settled by the design and not by the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two verdicts would change if the sample were ten times larger.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: judge a small but detectable effect against a practical yardstick
questions.stem: A programme moves scores by 0.3 points on a scale where a 5 point shift is the smallest one the organisation treats as worthwhile. What is the fairest description?

options.text: Detectable in the data but too small to be worth acting on here
Significant, so the programme is worth adopting straight away
options.misconception: assumes a reliable detection settles the question of value

options.text: Too small to be worth reporting, so the result should be dropped
options.misconception: lets a practical yardstick erase a real finding from the write-up

options.text: Worth acting on, since any reliably detected change carries value
options.misconception: treats any detectable change as automatically worth acting on

questions.explanation: Detection and value are separate questions, and a big enough study can detect a 0.3 point shift while the organisation's own 5 point threshold says the shift would not repay the cost of running the programme. The finding still belongs in the report, because the result is a fact about the world, and any reliably detected change is not automatically a change worth paying for.
questions.hint: Ask what the organisation said a worthwhile change would look like on this scale.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of an association for causal claims
questions.stem: Across 40 districts, spending per pupil and test scores correlate at 0.55. What does that figure establish?

options.text: The two move together across districts, with no cause or direction shown
Higher spending causes higher scores, since the link is moderately strong
options.misconception: reads a moderate association as a cause in one direction

options.text: Scores cause spending, since richer results may attract more money
options.misconception: reverses the direction to fit a preferred story about money

options.text: Neither causes the other, since every association of this size is spurious
options.misconception: dismisses a real association as though all such links were artefacts

questions.explanation: A correlation describes how two quantities move together and says nothing about which one drives the other, because a third factor such as family income can raise both school spending and results, and reversing the direction is equally available on the same data. Nothing here is spurious either, since districts that spend more really do tend to score higher, and what is missing is a design that separates spending from everything that travels with it.
questions.hint: Ask what other factor could raise both quantities at the same time.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: name the structure that defeats a causal reading of an association
questions.stem: Households owning more plants report lower stress scores. What stops this being a causal claim about plants?

options.text: A factor such as income could raise plant ownership and lower stress
A measurement problem, since stress is scored on a self-report scale
options.misconception: reaches for a scoring problem when the gap is in the causal structure

options.text: A recruitment problem, since plant owners volunteer for such studies
options.misconception: blames who signed up rather than what drives both variables

options.text: A power problem, since too few households were studied for the link
options.misconception: uses a small sample to explain away a shared third factor

questions.explanation: A third factor sitting behind both variables makes the association real and the causal story wrong, and higher income plausibly buys more plants while also buying sleep, space, and other things that lower stress, so the plants may be a marker rather than a cause. Self-report scoring and recruitment can both add problems, but neither of them is what makes the causal reading unsafe, and the size of the sample changes only how tight the estimate is.
questions.hint: Ask what else a household with more money would have besides plants.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why an unassigned comparison cannot support cause
questions.stem: A survey finds that people attending a weekly class report more friends than those who do not. Why is a causal claim not licensed?

options.text: Nobody assigned the classes, so a prior difference could drive both
The sample was too small, so no association of this kind can be causal
options.misconception: lets sample size decide whether a design supports cause

options.text: Friendship was self-reported, which disqualifies it for causal use
options.misconception: treats a self-report measure as barring causal inference

options.text: Attendees were volunteers, so the two groups were not comparable
options.misconception: confuses who took part with whether anything was assigned

questions.explanation: People who join a weekly class may already have more friends, and more time and confidence, and that pre-existing difference would show up as an association whether or not the class does anything, so without assignment the class and the friendship cannot be separated. Sample size affects precision, self-report affects the measure, and volunteering affects who responded, but none of those is the reason the causal step fails.
questions.hint: Ask what the participants already differed in before the class began.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify a comparison group that differs systematically from the treated one
questions.stem: A new course is piloted in one school while a neighbouring school keeps the old course. What is the main problem with the comparison?

options.text: The two schools were not alike, so any gap may predate the course
Only one school took the course, so the treated group is too small
options.misconception: counts sites rather than asking whether the groups were alike

options.text: The neighbouring school has older pupils, which matters only for precision
options.misconception: treats a real group difference as a question of precision

options.text: Two schools is too few to detect a difference of any size
options.misconception: confuses few sites with an absence of detectable difference

questions.explanation: A comparison group earns its name by being alike on everything that matters, and two different schools can differ in intake, staffing, funding, and neighbourhood, so a score gap between them is a gap between schools as much as anything to do with the course. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify what disclosure informed consent actually requires
questions.stem: For a study to be properly consented, participants must be told, in terms they can follow,

options.text: The purpose, the procedures, the risks, and the right to withdraw
The full set of results in advance, and the source of the funding
options.misconception: demands advance disclosure of results that do not yet exist

options.text: Only that research is involved, with the details kept brief
options.misconception: treats a bare mention of research as though disclosure were satisfied

options.text: The names of the researchers, and nothing about the procedures
options.misconception: reduces disclosure to staff names while omitting the procedures

questions.explanation: Consent has to be informed, which means the person learns what the study is for, what will be done to them, what could go wrong, and that they can stop at any point without penalty, and it has to be voluntary, which means understanding the terms is a precondition rather than a formality. Results do not exist yet at the point of consent, a bare mention of research discloses nothing actionable, and the researcher's name is not a substitute for describing the procedure.
questions.hint: Ask what a person needs to know to decide whether taking part suits them.

questions.learningObjective: identify what an ethics review board examines before data collection
questions.stem: Before a study begins, an institutional review board examines the proposal. What is it weighing?

options.text: The consent process, the risks against benefits, and who is selected
Only whether the grant budget covers the cost of the fieldwork
options.misconception: reduces an ethics review to a budget question

options.text: Only whether the findings will generalise to a wider population
options.misconception: treats generalisability as the only thing an ethics review weighs

options.text: Only whether the report will credit the institution correctly
options.misconception: swaps an ethics review for a credit and attribution check

questions.explanation: The board's question is whether the study is acceptable to conduct, which turns on whether consent will be genuine, whether the risks to participants are proportionate to what the work can gain, and whether the selection of people is fair and avoids pressuring a vulnerable group into taking part. Budgets, generalisability, and attribution are real matters but they are not what the review is set up to protect participants from.
questions.hint: Ask what could go wrong for a participant if the answer were careless.

questions.learningObjective: state when a deception study owes its participants an explanation
questions.stem: A study misled participants about a room's noise level and the findings depended on them believing it. When does the debriefing obligation fall due?

options.text: Promptly after they take part, so the false belief can be corrected
Only if a participant directly asks whether they were misled
options.misconception: makes disclosure depend on whether a participant happens to ask

options.text: Once the whole study is over and the data have been written up
options.misconception: defers correction until the analysis and report are already done

options.text: Only where the deception caused visible distress to someone
options.misconception: ties the obligation to harm rather than to the deception itself

questions.explanation: Participants who were deliberately misled are owed the truth as soon as the data are collected, because leaving someone to act on a false belief about what happened to them in the study is a harm in its own right, and the debriefing is also what makes the earlier consent defensible. Waiting for someone to ask transfers the burden to the person who was deceived, waiting for the write-up leaves the belief standing, and the obligation does not depend on whether anyone was visibly upset.
questions.hint: Ask how long a participant should be left holding a belief the study planted.

Reporting a result that turns out not to be significant at all
options.misconception: believes registration blocks an honest null result from being written up

options.text: Rewording a consent form to make it easier to follow
options.misconception: confuses plain-language revision with changing the analysis plan

options.text: Adding an author who later contributed to the analysis
options.misconception: treats ordinary authorship credit as a form of outcome-chasing

questions.explanation: Registering fixes in advance which analyses count and which data get excluded, so the analyst cannot go shopping through the results for a version that flatters the hypothesis, and any later change has to be reported as a deviation. A null result is still a result and belongs in the write-up, revising the wording of a consent form for clarity is not a change to the analysis, and credit for real intellectual work is unrelated to whether the data cooperated.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions an analyst would most want to make only after seeing the numbers.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: identify the evidence a study needs about whether its manipulation took
questions.stem: Half the participants are told to imagine a childhood home and half a beach, then everyone scores their mood on a twenty-item scale, with no record of whether the instructions worked. What is missing?

options.text: A manipulation check, evidence the instructions changed what they targeted
A second outcome scale, since one list cannot capture any mood at all
options.misconception: calls for another measurement scale instead of proof the manipulation worked

options.text: A larger sample, since the groups will be too small to compare fairly
options.misconception: presumes an unverified manipulation is a sample size problem

options.text: A consent form, since imagining a place carries physical risk to people
options.misconception: treats a mental-imagery task as though it carried physical risk

questions.explanation: A manipulation check asks whether the instruction actually produced the state it was meant to produce, and without one a null result cannot be read at all, because the instructions may simply have failed and a mood scale cannot tell that apart from an instruction that worked and did nothing. Adding scales or participants does not supply that evidence, and asking someone to picture a place carries no physical risk that a consent form would need to cover.
questions.hint: Ask how the study would tell a failed instruction from a failed effect.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a post hoc exclusion can manufacture a result
questions.stem: After seeing the results, a team drops three participants whose scores sit more than three deviations from the mean, and the main claim then holds. What is the concern?

options.text: The rule was chosen after the results, so it can select for the answer
Nothing, since an extreme score is a data error by definition
options.misconception: assumes an extreme value is automatically a mistake rather than a real case

options.text: Nothing, since three cases out of two hundred cannot change a result
options.misconception: judges an exclusion by how few cases it drops rather than by when it was set

options.text: Only that the three dropped cases were not listed in the report
options.misconception: reduces the problem to a reporting omission rather than the rule itself

questions.explanation: A rule fixed before the data cannot pick a side, but a rule invented afterwards can be shaped until the desired claim survives, and here the exclusion appears at exactly the point where it rescued the conclusion. Extreme values are sometimes genuine, so a pre-set rule would need a reason tied to the measurement rather than to its position in the distribution, and how few cases were removed says nothing about whether the decision was made in good faith.

questions.stem: A review calls the field divided in two and cites the five studies reporting an effect while citing none of the eleven that found none. What has gone wrong?

It is too short, since a proper review needs fifty citations at least
options.misconception: judges a review by its citation count rather than by its coverage

options.text: It is too old, since the cited work all predates a decade of research
options.misconception: faults a review for its date span with no evidence of staleness

options.text: It is unbalanced, since both camps need the same number of authors
options.misconception: confuses a count of agreeing studies with a balance of viewpoints

questions.explanation: A review is a map of the evidence, and printing only the studies that reported an effect while omitting the larger set of null findings turns the map into an argument, leaving the reader to conclude a live controversy where the record may actually be settled. Nothing turns on how many citations there are, how recent they are, or how many authors each camp has, since the defect is the omission of studies that exist.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would conclude that the eleven omitted studies would have shown.

The source is too old, so it cannot support a present-day claim
options.misconception: rejects a source on its date without reading what it says

options.text: The source is too brief, so it cannot support a full claim
options.misconception: rejects a source on its length without reading what it says

options.text: The claim is widely known, so it needs no source at all
options.misconception: waives the need to check a source when a claim sounds familiar

questions.explanation: A citation transfers the reader's trust, so pointing at work that studied a different technique on a different task lends the appearance of evidence to a claim that has none, and a careful reader who opens the source will find the mismatch at once. The age and length of a reference are beside the point, since a short recent paper can support a claim perfectly well, and a claim sounding well known is a reason to find a source rather than to skip one.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would find if they opened the cited article.

questions.learningObjective: judge whether a deception study discharged its debriefing duty
questions.stem: Participants are told the alarm sounded during a task when it did not, and the study sends a general thank-you note six months later without explaining the alarm. What is wrong?

options.text: The false belief was never corrected, so consent rested on a fiction
The delay was too long, since the note should arrive within one week
options.misconception: objects to the timing while ignoring that nothing was explained

options.text: Nothing, since no participant reported being troubled by the alarm
options.misconception: waives the duty because nobody has yet objected

options.text: Nothing, since the deception was mild and lasted only one task
options.misconception: waives the duty because the deception was small or brief

questions.explanation: A debriefing has to correct the specific false belief the study planted, and a general thank-you note leaves each participant still believing the alarm was part of their task, so the deception stays in place and the consent that allowed it was never put right. options.misconception: objects to the data format when the missing control is the real problem

options.text: The comparison covers one clinic, so the result cannot be generalised
options.misconception: calls a generalisability limit the decisive problem in this design

options.text: The comparison relies on last year, so the figures must already be out of date
options.misconception: treats recency as the flaw rather than the absent concurrent control

questions.explanation: Comparing this year against last year puts the new procedure and a dozen other changes on one side of the comparison, including staffing, caseload, and season, so a gap in the figures cannot be pinned on the procedure at all. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: read a standardised difference against a stated practical bar
questions.stem: A programme trial reports a standardised mean difference of 0.18 with 200 participants per group, and the field treats 0.50 as the smallest effect worth acting on. First say what 0.18 means, then say whether it clears that bar.

options.text: A gap of 0.18 pooled deviations, short of the 0.50 bar
A gap of 0.18 pooled deviations, which clears the 0.50 bar as stated
options.misconception: reverses the comparison, treating a small figure as clearing a larger bar

options.text: A gap of 0.50 pooled deviations, which sits exactly on the bar
options.misconception: replaces the reported size with the threshold it was measured against

options.text: A gap of 0.18 raw points, unjudgeable without the outcome's units
options.misconception: reads a standardised figure as a raw score with no reference to spread

questions.explanation: A standardised difference states the gap in units of the measure's own spread, so 0.18 means the groups differ by about a fifth of one pooled deviation, which on this field's own reckoning is well short of the 0.50 that would justify action. The 200 per group is what made the gap detectable at all, and the number is not a count of points on some unstated scale, so substituting the threshold for the result answers a different question.
questions.hint: Compare the reported figure with the bar rather than the other way round.

questions.learningObjective: name the ethical requirement breached when a stated term is not honoured
questions.stem: A study tells participants on the consent form that they will receive a modest payment, and then the budget is frozen and nobody is paid. First name what was breached, then say what should have happened.

options.text: The agreement to stated terms, which the researchers had to honour
Informed consent, since the payment was never described to the panel
options.misconception: picks a disclosure fault for a breach of an already-stated term

options.text: Debriefing, since participants were never told the study was finished
options.misconception: reaches for debriefing when the problem is keeping a commitment

options.text: Anonymity, since the payment records identified who took part
options.misconception: confuses a broken promise with a failure to protect identity

questions.explanation: Consent is an agreement to stated terms, so a payment described on the form is part of what the participant accepted and cannot be withdrawn afterwards simply because the money ran out. Disclosure was not the failure here since the terms were properly stated, debriefing concerns correcting false beliefs about the study, and nothing about the payment records bears on identity protection.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a real limitation from a generic caveat

It is too short, since a limitations section needs a full page
options.misconception: judges a limitations section by length rather than by content

options.text: It admits the study failed, so no results may be reported at all
options.misconception: treats honest caveats as grounds for withholding the results

options.text: It looks forward to future work, so it should precede the study
options.misconception: objects to a forward-looking sentence instead of the missing specifics

questions.explanation: A limitation names a choice the researchers made and what that choice does to the claim, whereas calling for larger samples offers a remedy rather than an accounting, and a bigger sample fixes precision without touching a biased frame or a confounded comparison. questions.learningObjective: reject a causal conclusion that outruns an observational design
questions.stem: A survey of 900 adults finds that daily tea drinkers report lower blood pressure, and the report concludes that drinking tea lowers blood pressure. What is wrong?

options.text: Nobody was assigned a tea habit, so a shared cause could drive both
The sample is large, so the finding must hold in other settings
options.misconception: treats a large sample as settling the causal question

options.text: Pressure was measured once, so the finding cannot be interpreted
options.misconception: objects to measurement frequency while ignoring the missing assignment

options.text: Drinking tea is a habit, and habits cannot be studied scientifically
options.misconception: dismisses a whole class of studyable variables on principle

questions.explanation: A survey records what people already do, and the people who drink tea daily differ before any tea is measured, in diet, income, activity, and health awareness, and any of those could lower blood pressure on its own, so the design cannot separate the habit from the lives that go with it. Nine hundred respondents tighten the estimate without touching that, a single reading is a normal feature of survey work, and studying habits is precisely what observational designs are for.

options.text: Attendance measures engagement, so it cannot be the cause of itself
The comparison group was not random, so the gap proves nothing
options.misconception: replaces the specific reversal with a general complaint about design

options.text: Both groups attended plenty, so the gap must be a recording error
options.misconception: treats substantial attendance in both groups as proof the gap is unreal

options.text: Attendance is a behaviour, and only attitudes can be caused
options.misconception: rules out behaviour as an outcome on the grounds it is not an attitude

questions.explanation: The number of sessions attended is how the report describes engagement with the programme, and a summary of the outcome cannot be the reason the outcome happened, so the sentence has the arrow running backwards. questions.hint: Ask whether the thing named as the cause is simply a restatement of the effect.

questions.learningObjective: diagnose a family of comparisons reported without adjustment
questions.stem: A report presents 40 separate outcome comparisons, marks 5 as significant, and reports each at a 0.04 level with no adjustment. What is the problem?

options.text: Forty tests at that level produce several lucky hits with nothing behind them
Five hits out of 40 is a normal rate, so nothing here needs comment
options.misconception: treats five hits in forty as plausible without a chance benchmark

options.text: A 0.04 level is stricter than 0.05, so the results are safely protected
options.misconception: believes a slightly stricter per-test level protects the family

options.text: The forty should have been replaced by one combined outcome measure
options.misconception: prescribes a different measurement instead of correcting the testing

questions.explanation: Forty independent tests at 0.04 would throw up about 1.6 significant results by luck when nothing at all is happening, and at 0.05 it is close to 2, so five hits needs a real explanation that the report does not provide. questions.hint: Ask how many of those forty would come out significant if the programme did nothing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Computing and then correcting a family of tests
questions.learningObjective: compute a family error rate and the per-test level that fixes it
questions.stem: A team runs 20 independent tests at a 5 percent level each and wants the chance of any one false positive held to 5 percent. First compute that chance as it currently stands, then give the per-test level the family needs.

options.text: About 0.64, with a per-test level of 0.0025
About 0.36, with a per-test level of 0.0025
options.misconception: reads the chance that all tests miss as the false-positive chance

options.text: About 0.64, with a per-test level of 0.05
options.misconception: computes the chance correctly then leaves each test at the full level

options.text: About 0.05, with a per-test level of 0.05
options.misconception: assumes the per-test level alone already caps the whole family

questions.explanation: The chance that all twenty tests miss is 0.95 to the twentieth, which is 0.3585, so the chance that at least one hits by luck is 1 minus that, or about 0.64, and holding the family to 5 percent means dividing 0.05 across the twenty tests, which leaves 0.0025 each. The 0.36 figure is the chance of no false positives at all, which is the other side of the same coin, and leaving each test at 0.05 is exactly the situation the correction exists to fix.
questions.hint: First find the chance that none of the twenty hits, then take the other side.

questions.learningObjective: state what an interval crossing the null permits and forbids

options.text: Zero is outside, so the effect is proven to equal 0.4 units
options.misconception: takes the midpoint of an interval for a proven effect size

questions.topic: What a comparison group on the same schedule adds

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why regression to the mean flatters treatments
questions.learningObjective: explain an apparent improvement that needs no treatment
questions.stem: A clinic takes the 200 patients whose first pain score is the highest recorded and treats all of them. Six weeks later their average pain is lower. Explain why this drop does not show that the treatment works.

answer.exemplar: The clinic chose its patients on the first reading, and that reading is part real pain and part whatever the scale and the moment added that day, so the selected group starts with an unusual quantity of measurement error folded into it. On the second visit that error does not repeat, and the average falls without anything having been done differently, which is regression to the mean. A group picked the same way and given nothing would show much the same decline, so the before-and-after figure cannot separate the treatment from the arithmetic of choosing the worst starting scores. The remedy is a comparison group selected on the same first readings, or randomising who is treated, not a longer study of the same before-and-after pattern.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the group was selected on an extreme first reading, explains that the error in that reading does not repeat, and concludes that an untreated group chosen the same way would show a similar decline.
questions.hint: Ask what the first reading contributed to the group besides real pain.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain how a reliable finding can still be too small to matter
questions.stem: A study of 4000 participants finds a programme lowers a symptom score by 0.08 on a 100 point scale, while a comparison drug lowers it by 2.5. Explain how the finding can be real and still not worth acting on.

answer.exemplar: The two questions are settled by different arithmetic. With 4000 people the noise around an estimate is narrow enough that a shift of 0.08 is unlikely to be an accident, so the finding clears the significance bar while sitting far below the 2.5 the comparison drug achieves, and nobody would reorganise a service around a reduction that small. The same 0.08 measured on 50 people would probably not be detectable at all, which is why a finding whose significance rides on the sample size is not thereby a finding that carries weight. The report has to carry both numbers, and a reader shown only the significance verdict would draw the wrong conclusion about whether acting is worthwhile.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates the question of detection from the question of value, notes that a very large sample can make a tiny difference significant, and explains that a small effect judged against a larger achieved one may not justify the cost.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the same 0.08 shift if the study had enrolled far fewer people.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why observational designs stop short of cause
questions.learningObjective: explain what an association leaves undetermined and what would settle it
questions.stem: A survey finds that districts with more pedestrian crossings have lower pedestrian injury rates. Explain why the association does not license the claim that the crossings reduced injuries.

answer.exemplar: Districts that install crossings are districts that were already worried about pedestrian injuries, so a shared concern sits behind both the crossings and the rate they are paired with, and it can lower that rate with the crossings doing nothing. A survey also cannot stop income, street width, vehicle speed, or lighting from moving with the same decision, and each of those could carry the effect on its own. The honest reading is that districts with more crossings had lower rates, with cause and direction left open. A design that could settle the question would have to assign crossings to otherwise comparable districts and watch injury rates over time, and a survey has no way to perform that assignment.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies a plausible factor behind both the crossings and the injury rate, notes that other differences travel with the decision to build, and explains that only an assignment of crossings could separate the crossings from those reasons.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of district decides to put in a crossing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: explain how a public record constrains later analytic choices
questions.stem: A team registered its hypotheses, sample size, and exclusion rules publicly, then finds a surprising pattern and runs a fresh analysis on it. Explain what the registration does to the standing of that second analysis.

answer.exemplar: A surprising pattern is exactly the situation a registered plan is built for, because a result nobody predicted is the one most likely to be chased through variations of the analysis until something clears the bar. With the plan on public record the second analysis can still be run, but it inherits a burden of proof it would not otherwise carry: a reader can check whether the exclusions and the test were fixed beforehand, and the new analysis must be labelled exploratory and kept apart from the confirmatory result. That label costs the team its headline, because an exploratory finding is a hypothesis for the next study rather than a conclusion from this one. Without the record, nothing in the paper would show which analyses were planned and which were found, which is the whole problem registration exists to remove.

questions.explanation: A strong response says the surprising result is the case registration targets, explains that the new analysis can run but must be labelled exploratory, and notes that the public record is what lets a reader tell planned analysis from discovered analysis.
questions.hint: Ask how a reader could tell which analyses were planned and which were found.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a limitations section has to do
questions.learningObjective: explain what a limitations section owes the next reader
questions.stem: A report's limitations section contains only generic caveats. Explain what a limitations section has to do that a list of generic caveats does not.

answer.exemplar: A limitation is a statement about a choice the researchers made and its consequence for the claim, so noting that all participants came from one campus and that the estimate may not describe distant ones ties a specific decision to the specific conclusion it weakens. Generic caveats substitute a remedy for an accounting, since asking for larger samples fixes precision and leaves a biased frame, a confounded comparison, or a measure that missed part of the construct entirely untouched. The section also has to be usable by the next reader, who needs to know which findings survive the caveat and which do not, and that requires naming the specific threat rather than gesturing at rigour in general.

questions.explanation: A strong response says a limitation names a design choice and its consequence, contrasts that with a remedy that fixes something other than the actual problem, and explains that the section exists to tell a reader which findings still stand.
questions.hint: Ask which findings a reader could still rely on after reading each sentence.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a null result needs a manipulation check
questions.learningObjective: explain the two readings a null result can have
questions.stem: A study puts half its participants into a writing task and half into a reading task, then finds no difference in recall scores. Explain why the report needs a manipulation check before drawing any conclusion from that null result.

answer.exemplar: A null result carries two quite different meanings and the design data separate them. If the writing task produced the deeper processing the theory relies on, then the absence of a recall difference is a real and unwelcome fact about the theory. If participants skimmed both tasks equally, the manipulation never happened and the study has learned nothing about processing, only about compliance. Without a check the two are indistinguishable in the results, and the pull is always toward the first reading because it is the one that makes an interesting paragraph. A short measure of how deeply each group engaged, or of whether they followed the instruction, is cheap to collect and turns an uninterpretable null into a definite statement about the theory.

questions.explanation: A strong response lays out the two readings of a null result, explains that only the manipulation check distinguishes them, and notes that the second reading is at least as likely as the first.
questions.hint: Ask whether the null means the theory failed or the instruction failed, and how to tell.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: From registered plan to reported result
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that carry a study from plan to reported result
questions.stem: A team has registered its plan and collected its data. Put these steps in the order that should be carried out.

options.text: Apply the registered exclusion rules to the collected data
Run the registered analysis and check the manipulation took
Report the exclusions and any departure from the plan
Report the effect size with its interval beside the test
State what the design can and cannot support

questions.explanation: Exclusions are applied before the outcomes are examined, or they stop being a rule and become a choice, and the manipulation check is read alongside the analysis because a null is uninterpretable without it. The reader then learns what was removed and what departed from the plan, sees the effect with the interval that describes its precision, and only then reads a claim the design can actually carry.
questions.hint: Decisions about which data to keep must precede looking at what the data say.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence a debriefing so the deception is properly corrected
questions.stem: A deception study has finished collecting data. Put these steps in the order that discharges the obligation properly.

options.text: Debrief each participant promptly and correct the false belief
Answer their questions and offer withdrawal of their data
Provide support and a route to ask more questions later
Record the debriefing and report it in the write-up

questions.explanation: The false belief has to be corrected first and promptly, because leaving it in place is the harm, and only once it is corrected does it make sense to answer questions and let a participant withdraw data that were gathered under the deception. Support and a later contact route come after that, and recording what was covered lets an ethics reader check the duty was actually discharged rather than merely intended.
questions.hint: Start with the belief that has to be removed from each person.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Turning results into a defensible claim
questions.learningObjective: sequence the checks that stand between results and a claim
questions.stem: A finished study's results are in hand. Put these steps in the order that turns them into a claim a reader should trust.

options.text: Check the manipulation produced what it was meant to produce
Check who was lost and whether the losses were related
Compute the effect size and the interval around it
Weigh the effect against what would be worth acting on
State the claim no further than the design reaches

questions.explanation: The first two checks ask whether the study measured what it meant to and whether the people analysed are still the people who started, and a claim that survives neither is not rescued by statistics. Only once those hold does it make sense to state the effect with its interval, weigh that effect against what acting would require, and finally write a conclusion whose reach matches the design that produced it.
questions.hint: Two questions about whether the study means what it says come before any arithmetic.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: sequence the sections of a report from method to claim
questions.stem: Put these elements of a research report in the order they should be written, from what the study is to what it claims.

options.text: State the design, the sample, and the measures used
Give the result with its interval and its exclusions
Explain which threats to validity the design leaves
Compare the finding with prior work in the area
State the limits, including where the result should not go

questions.explanation: A reader cannot judge a result without the design, the sample, and the measures that produced it, so those come first, followed by the result with the interval and the exclusions that shaped it. The threats that remain explain what the number can survive, the comparison with prior work places it in the field, and only after all of that does the final statement say how far the finding should travel.
questions.hint: A reader needs the method in hand before the number means anything.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A significant result of trivial size
questions.learningObjective: weigh a reliable finding against a stated threshold for action
questions.stem: A report gives a value of 0.02 with an effect size of 0.10 from 3000 participants per group, and the field's smallest worthwhile effect is 0.40. What is the fair conclusion?

options.text: A real but tiny difference, too small to justify changing practice
A worthwhile difference, since a reliable result means the effect matters
options.misconception: reads a reliable detection as a statement about value

options.text: No difference at all, since an effect of 0.10 is well inside the noise
options.misconception: confuses a small effect with an effect indistinguishable from noise

options.text: An untested claim, since no effect can be judged at this sample size
options.misconception: denies that a very large sample can detect a small effect

questions.explanation: Three thousand participants per group is enough to separate a 0.10 effect from random scatter, so the difference is there, and the field's own yardstick says a change that small is not worth reorganising practice around. A small effect is not the same as no effect, and a very large sample is precisely what makes a small effect detectable rather than untestable, so the report has to carry the size next to the test.
questions.hint: Ask what the field said a change worth acting on would look like.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An interval against a practical threshold
questions.learningObjective: judge a saving whose interval straddles the point of worth
questions.stem: A new triage rule cuts average waiting time by 4.0 minutes, with a 95 percent interval from 0.8 to 7.2, and the service's own smallest worthwhile saving is 5 minutes. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: The saving is real but the interval includes amounts not worth having
The saving clears the bar, since 4.0 sits close to the 5 minute mark
options.misconception: compares the estimate with the bar and ignores where the interval sits

options.text: The saving is worthless, since the lower end falls below the 5 minute mark
options.misconception: treats one end of the interval as settling the whole range

options.text: The saving is too uncertain, since the interval is far too wide to read
options.misconception: calls a wide interval uninterpretable when it plainly narrows the question

questions.explanation: Every value in the interval is a saving, so the rule does something, and 7.2 is above the 5 minute bar while 0.8 is well below it, which means the data are consistent with a change worth having and with one that is not, and the fair statement is that the saving is real and its size still needs pinning down. Comparing only the 4.0 estimate with the bar answers a different question, one end of the interval does not settle the range, and a wide interval is informative rather than unreadable.
questions.hint: Ask where the bar sits inside the two ends.
